title: Dievas and Velnias Create the World
source_ref: Lithuanian and Latvian cosmogonic tales collected in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries; comparative earth-diver scholarship
paragraphs: At the beginning there was only water, and above it the bright sky where Dievas lived. The sky god looked down on the restless deep, and beside him, or rising from it, was Velnias, the clever one, who could not sit still. Neither made the world alone. The old tales begin with the two of them together, before land, before shores, before anything that could be walked upon.

Dievas told Velnias to dive: 'Go down, bring up a handful of earth, and we will have a world.' Velnias went into the dark water, stayed a long time, and came back with sand in his hand, but he had kept a little in his mouth. Dievas scattered what he was given, and it spread and grew into fields and islands.

Then the hidden sand began to swell. Velnias's mouth filled, his cheeks stretched, and he could not speak. He spat the earth out, and it fell in lumps: hills, boulders, ridges and dry patches. This is why the land is not flat. The fields are Dievas's gift, but the stones and the bogs are the trickster's leftovers, and both belong to the world.

The story is not a single old text. Lithuanian and Latvian tales about the earth-diver were written down in the nineteenth century, and they differ: sometimes Velnias is a bird, sometimes a man, sometimes the devil of Christian teaching. The connected cosmogony is a modern reconstruction, and scholars still argue whether it is old Baltic tradition, a borrowed apocryphal story, or both.
notes: No Baltic creation text survives. The earth-diver cosmogony is reconstructed from Lithuanian and Latvian folk tales recorded in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, which vary in the role of Velnias (bird, man or devil) and in how much of the world he makes. Scholars debate whether the dualism is inherited Baltic tradition or owes something to Christian apocrypha and neighbouring steppe traditions.

title: Perkūnas and the Devil
source_ref: Lithuanian dainos and Latvian dainas; Jan Łasicki, De diis Samagitarum (1582); later folklore
paragraphs: Perkūnas lived in the sky and drove the thunder. His chariot rolled over the clouds, his axe flashed as lightning, and the oak was his tree. He was not a distant god. Farmers listened for his first storm of spring, when the sky opened and the rain came down on the fields. Thunder was the sound of him at work, and lightning was the blow.

Velnias, the trickster, was always near. He stole what was not his, hid in the reeds, and slipped away when the storm came. Perkūnas chased him across the sky. The devil turned himself into a tree, a stone, a fish, a black cat, a man, but each hiding place gave him away. People said the thunder was Perkūnas shouting: where are you?

When the axe found its mark, it split the oak or the rock where Velnias crouched. The blow scorched the bark and left the tree standing, wounded and holy. Then the rain fell. The first thunder of the year was a promise that the frost had lost, the grass would rise, and the cattle could go out. The storm was frightening, but it was also the beginning of summer.

The chase is known from dainos and dainas, from place names and from later peasant custom, not from a pagan narrative. Christian teaching made Velnias into the devil, and the old rival became evil in a new way. The Perkūnas who appears in songs is a storm god and a keeper of order, and the story of his pursuit is a reconstruction built from many short verses.
notes: No pagan Baltic text narrates the chase. The story is reconstructed from dainos and dainas, place names and later folklore in which Velnias has become the Christian devil. The details of the pursuit, the hiding places and the punishment vary, and the spring-rain meaning is a scholarly reading of the songs rather than an ancient explanation.

title: Saulė and Mėnulis
source_ref: Lithuanian dainos and Latvian dainas; Lithuanian ethnoastronomy
paragraphs: Saulė, the sun, and Mėnulis, the moon, were husband and wife. In the songs they are called mummy and daddy, a household pair who once lived together and now cross the sky by turns. Saulė wore a golden crown and drove a carriage of light; Mėnulis was pale and quiet, a silver boat on the night water. Their children were the stars and the earth.

Then came the quarrel. In one telling the couple could not agree about their daughter, the earth, and each wanted her for a different life. In another, Mėnulis was unfaithful and courted Aušrinė, the morning star. Saulė saw, and the marriage broke. The songs do not preach; they grieve, tease and scold, and they leave the blame moving between husband and wife.

Perkūnas came into the quarrel. He separated the pair, or punished Mėnulis by cutting him in two with a sword. That is why the moon is not whole. Sometimes Saulė herself strikes him with a silver whip, and sometimes she simply turns away and hides, and the night is dark. The waning moon is a husband losing his strength, or a share of his property given away; the waxing is his return.

The names shift between languages and regions: Saulė and Saule, Mėnulis and Mēness, Aušrinė and Auseklis. These are poetic, not doctrinal, figures. No Baltic priest wrote a chapter on the sun's marriage; the evidence is a great body of short songs, and the story here is a weaving of variants. It should be read as song, not scripture.
notes: The marriage and quarrel of Saulė and Mėnulis are known from many short songs, not from a fixed myth. Variants name the rival as Aušrinė or Auseklis, blame the moon or the sun, and explain the phases by a sword, a whip or a division of property. The retelling is a composite and should be read as poetry, not doctrine.

title: Jūratė and Kastytis
source_ref: Maironis, 'Jūratė ir Kastytis' in Pavasario balsai (1895); earlier nineteenth-century literary and folk material
paragraphs: Beneath the Baltic, in a palace of amber, lived Jūratė, queen of the sea. The walls glowed without lamps, the floors were clear gold, and the waves above were a roof of green glass. She ruled the fish and the deep water and wanted no human nets in her realm. On the shore near Palanga, a young fisherman named Kastytis cast his nets anyway.

Jūratė rose to stop him, and instead fell in love. She brought Kastytis down to the amber hall, where human and sea lived for a while as if the border between them did not exist. He was warm and mortal; she was older than the shore. The legend lingers on that impossible happiness, because it knows the price has not yet been paid.

Perkūnas saw. A goddess of the sea had taken a mortal man, and the order of things was broken. He struck the amber palace with lightning, and the hall shattered into pieces that the waves carried along the coast. Kastytis died. Jūratė was bound to the ruins, and her tears, or the fragments of her home, are the amber that people still find on the beach.

The popular story is not an ancient text. Maironis shaped it in the ballad 'Jūratė ir Kastytis', printed in Pavasario balsai in 1895, and an earlier literary version has been attributed to Liudvikas Adomas Jucevičius. Older folk material gave the sea queen and the amber, but the romance, the punishment and the tears owe much to nineteenth-century poetry. It is a modern legend with old roots.
notes: The popular narrative is a nineteenth-century literary shaping, not an ancient text. Maironis's ballad in Pavasario balsai (1895) fixed the romance, the punishment and the amber tears; an earlier literary version is attributed to Liudvikas Adomas Jucevičius. Older folk material supplies the sea queen and the amber, but the connected plot, and details such as whether Kastytis dies or Jūratė is chained, vary between retellings.

title: Eglė the Queen of Serpents
source_ref: Lithuanian folktale 'Eglė žalčių karalienė', first published in 1837; more than a hundred collected variants
paragraphs: Eglė bathed in the sea with her two sisters. When she came out, a grass snake was coiled in her clothes, and it spoke with a man's voice. It would give the clothes back only if she promised to marry it. Eglė laughed and promised, thinking a snake could not hold her to a word. Three days later thousands of snakes came to her parents' gate.

Her parents tried to cheat them, dressing a goose, a sheep and a cow as brides, but a cuckoo warned the snakes each time. At last Eglė was given up. On the shore she found not a snake but a handsome young man, Žilvinas, who took her to his palace under the sea. They had four children: Ąžuolas, Uosis, Beržas and little Drebulė.

Nine years passed before Eglė grew homesick. Žilvinas forbade her to go, then set three impossible tasks: spin an endless skein, wear out iron clogs, bake a cake without vessels. With a witch's help she did them all. Before she left, he taught her the call that only she and the children knew: if he lived, he would come as white milk foam; if dead, as black blood foam.

At home her twelve brothers wanted to keep her. They beat the sons, who would not tell the call, but frightened Drebulė told everything. The brothers called Žilvinas to the shore and cut him down with scythes. Eglė called, saw the blood foam, and in her grief cursed her children: the sons became oak, ash and birch, the daughter the trembling aspen, and Eglė herself a spruce.

title: Sovijus and the Journey of the Dead
source_ref: The Sovijus tale in the Slavonic Chronograph (1261); the sixteenth-century Sudovian Book; later studies by Greimas, Beresnevičius and Vėlius
paragraphs: Sovijus was a hunter, and the tale begins with a boar. He killed it and set aside nine spleens for his children to cook, but they ate them. His anger would not cool. He set out for the land of the dead, meaning to see what lay beyond, and his sons were drawn into the journey.

The road ran through gates. He passed eight of them, and at the ninth he needed help; one son gave it, and the others turned on that son for helping. Beyond the gates were the paths the dead must walk, the places where souls gather, and the powers that receive them. The living were not meant to walk this road, and what Sovijus saw there became his people's knowledge of the dead.

His son laid Sovijus's body in the earth, and Sovijus was not at rest. He laid it in a tree, and that was no better. Then he laid it on a pyre, and Sovijus slept 'like a child in a cradle'. From that the people learned to burn their dead, to give them grave goods, and to hold the funeral feast. The three burials are three ages remembered in one story.

The story survives in a Slavonic chronograph of 1261; later chroniclers, including sixteenth-century compilers, repeated and expanded it, and the Sudovian Book describes the funerals it was thought to justify. Scholars read Sovijus as a charter for cremation, a guide of souls, or a figure of the sun. None of these readings is certain. The gates, the paths and even Sovijus himself are reconstructed across a long chain of copying.
notes: The Sovijus tale is preserved in the 1261 Slavonic Chronograph, a translation of John Malalas, not in a contemporary Baltic text. Sixteenth-century compilers repeated it, and the Sudovian Book describes the funeral customs later attached to him. The gates, the number nine, the three burials and Sovijus's own status (culture hero, god or euhemerised figure) are interpreted very differently; the narrative here is a reconstruction.
